title: Unifying PingCastle, Microsoft Zero Trust, and SCuBA Through the DoW Zero Trust Activity Model
excerpt: Executive Summary
content:
Executive Summary

The DoW Zero Trust roadmap provides a common direction for modernization, but its 152 activities can be difficult to apply in a hybrid enterprise with legacy systems, mission constraints, and limited funding. I see value in the framework, especially its emphasis on continuous verification and least privilege. I also worry that tracking activities can take attention away from reducing attack paths and getting identity fundamentals right.

One practical problem is that assessments report on different parts of the environment. PingCastle examines Active Directory exposure, Microsoft Zero Trust Assessment covers cloud identity and access, and SCuBA checks configuration against secure baselines. Their findings may point to the same underlying weakness without being duplicates. Reading the reports separately makes it harder to assign ownership and decide what deserves attention first.

My approach maps those findings to shared DoW Zero Trust activities. Teams run the tools

title: AgentBench: A Framework for AI Agent Control Validation
excerpt: Executive Summary
content:
Executive Summary

Security reviews for AI agents often leave evidence scattered across screenshots, spreadsheets, and test results. I built AgentBench to bring control validation into one place so a team can see what was tested, how the agent responded, and what remains outside the assessment. It draws on frameworks including NIST AI RMF, AIUC-1, and the OWASP LLM Top 10, while focusing on controls that can be exercised directly.

The distinction between governance, validation, and enforcement matters. Governance sets expectations. AgentBench tests behavior against those expectations, including attempts to cross data or authorization boundaries. Runtime controls constrain what the agent can do in production. Each has a different job, and a favorable test result does not replace the others.

Scope changes what a result means. A retrieval-augmented agent, for example, has different risks from a code-generation or autonomous agent, and sensitive leakage tests may belong only in controlle

title: Spycraft 2.1: From Wallets to Structure in Bitcoin Transaction Graphs
excerpt: Executive Summary
content:
Executive Summary

The VADER collection included Bitcoin wallet and transaction identifiers associated with dead drop resolvers. I wanted to see what those indicators looked like as a network rather than a list. Starting with 14 wallets and 23 transactions, I enriched the data and expanded it one hop. The resulting graph contained 993 nodes, 1,579 edges, and 41 wallets.

A small number of hubs carried much of the observed activity, while many surrounding wallets appeared less often. The expanded graph also produced 540 related-wallet links. Some decoded values repeated across transactions, and the ten seed wallets with decoded activity had enough timestamp context to examine recurrence from mid-2017 through early 2021. These patterns give an investigator places to look for continuity and change.

title: Measuring Malware Cluster Persistence in 2025: What Actually Stayed Active?
excerpt: Threat data is noisy, and headline trend charts often hide what is actually sticking around. I wanted to answer a practical question: which malware activity really persisted over time, and what did that persistence look
content:
Threat data is noisy, and headline trend charts often hide what is actually sticking around. I wanted to answer a practical question: which malware activity really persisted over time, and what did that persistence look like in behavior?

Executive Summary

I analyzed 120,000 samples collected from November 2024 through October 2025 to see which malware clusters persisted and whether their behavior stayed consistent. After deduplication, family-name normalization, and behavioral mapping, the data produced 861 normalized clusters. Ten accounted for 89.4% of observed samples, and the main concentration patterns remained stable as I changed detection-consensus thresholds. The major indicators also converged at around 35,000 samples.

title: The Case for Proof-of-Value in Security Partnerships
excerpt: Executive Summary
content:
Executive Summary

I came to proof-of-value from an onboarding experience that did not go as expected. The product looked promising, but after the contract was signed, getting it into use felt more like trial and error than a guided process. I had not led a proof-of-value myself, so this is a reflection on what I would do differently rather than a report of a completed pilot.

A useful pilot should show how a product and its vendor work with the people who will operate it. That includes security analysts, enterprise engineers, and networking teams. Clear setup documentation, realistic milestones, honest discussion of coverage gaps, and peer feedback all help establish whether the organization can use the capability without relying on the vendor for every step.

title: From Anomalous Traffic to Spycraft 2.0
excerpt: Executive Summary
content:
Executive Summary

The investigation began with a malware sample connecting to X.com rather than directly to its known command-and-control server. That traffic led us to a dead drop resolver: malware retrieves an encoded address from a legitimate web service, decodes it, and uses the result to find its operator’s infrastructure. The web service provides useful cover, and removing one dead drop does not prevent the operator from creating another.

With VADER, we looked for a way to address the decoding method instead of chasing each endpoint separately. We traced the path from a web request to a command-and-control connection, isolated the code that transforms the retrieved data, and used symbolic analysis to recover a reusable decoding recipe. In the Mudrop case, that recipe helped us find three previously unknown dead drops in WordPress posts.

Overview

Personal research/brand site for EmpiricalDefense (https://empiricaldefense.com), built with Jekyll 4 on t
content:
This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

Overview

Personal research/brand site for EmpiricalDefense (https://empiricaldefense.com), built with Jekyll 4 on the Hydejack 9 theme (jekyll-theme-hydejack gem). Most work here is content (blog posts, publications, talks) plus targeted overrides of the theme’s layouts/includes. There is no test suite; the build plus HTML Proofer is the validation.

Commands

Ruby 3.2.3 (via rbenv, see .ruby-version), Bundler 2.2.3, gems installed locally to vendor/bundle.

bundle config set --local path 'vendor/bundle'
bundle _2.2.3_ install

bundle exec jekyll serve                       # dev server at http://localhost:4000, auto-rebuilds
JEKYLL_ENV=production bundle exec jekyll build --trace   # production build (what CI runs)

# Validate output the way CI does (internal links/images/scripts only)
htmlproofer ./_site --disable-external \
  --ignore-files "/CHANGELOG/,/licenses/,/LICENSE/,/NOTIC
